source: a16z Podcast — Is AI a bubble? Data centers, GPUs, and the AI economy
summary: Frontier AI lab gross margins will be structurally lower than SaaS/internet-era margins due to compute intensity from scaling laws and test-time compute, but they can still be great businesses.
summary_extended: Baker argues that frontier AI lab gross margins will be structurally and permanently lower than the 70-80%+ margins characteristic of SaaS and internet-era software businesses, due to the inherent compute intensity embedded in scaling laws and the growing importance of test-time compute. The reasoning is grounded in Richard Sutton's 'Bitter Lesson' — the empirical observation that throwing more compute at problems consistently outperforms human-engineered solutions — meaning compute expenditure is not a temporary inefficiency but a permanent structural feature of frontier AI. However, Baker notes that frontier AI labs can still be exceptional businesses because OPEX can be dramatically lower than traditional software companies, potentially offsetting the gross margin compression and preserving strong operating margins. He sees no evidence that scaling laws or test-time compute will diminish in importance, making this a durable structural reality rather than a transitional phase. The investment implication is that investors should not benchmark frontier AI lab margins against SaaS comps, and that compute infrastructure suppliers (rather than model providers) may capture a disproportionate share of the value chain.
detail: Scaling laws and Richard Sutton's 'Bitter Lesson' mean frontier models are inherently more compute-intensive than SaaS. Gross margins will be structurally depressed for a long time. However, OPEX can be much lower, potentially squaring the circle. Baker does not see scaling laws or test-time compute importance changing.
confidence_evidence: Baker states this as a structural fact with no hedging language, grounded in first-principles reasoning about compute intensity.
